name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,625

clue.text: Politician recycling trite remarks, wasting a bit of time

indicators.note: to waste something is to throw it away, so some letters are discarded from the material
recycled material is broken down and remade into something new, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time; only one of the two Ts goes

explanation.surface: A politician churns out the same old platitudes while dodging the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop one T from TRITE REMARKS and the remaining eleven letters rearrange into KEIR STARMER; the surface is a fair jibe at any speechmaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Keir Starmer is the Labour leader who became British Prime Minister in 2024, an example of a career politician.

clue.text: 24's friend visiting coffee producer (not a place for bourbon)

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone else's home, so one piece sits within another
'not' tells us to leave out the letter named right after it

blocks.note: 24 across is ROBIN HOOD, whose companion was Friar Tuck
Kenya is a major coffee-growing country

explanation.surface: A friend drops in on a coffee grower, and the parenthesis warns this is no whiskey town.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis is split: 'not a' removes the A from KENYA, while 'place for bourbon' is the definition. The cross-reference to 24 gives the merry man Friar Tuck.
explanation.definitionFit: Kentucky is the American state where most bourbon whiskey is distilled, giving the spirit its traditional home.

clue.text: The first Tsar? I haven't a clue

definitions.note: a self-deprecating admission, read as 'I'm hopeless'; the answer is a name

blocks.note: first meaning: the sixteenth-century Russian ruler who was first crowned Tsar of all Russia
second meaning: a confession of being useless at something, split as 'I've an' plus 'the terrible'

explanation.walkthrough: Read the name as 'I've an, the terrible...': someone admitting they are terrible, as one is when one hasn't a clue. The setter jokes that the clue itself barely counts as one.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan IV of Russia was crowned the first Tsar in 1547, and his epithet doubles as a cheerful confession of incompetence.

clue.text: Male escort Ewan stripped in a den of vice

indicators.note: stripping removes the outer layer, leaving only the inner letters
one thing placed in another ends up enclosed by it

blocks.note: the name with its first and last letters removed
sin is vice, the place where wickedness dwells

explanation.surface: A man called Ewan works as a naked escort in a seedy establishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Male escort' sounds sleazy here, but the old word means a young suitor who walks out with his sweetheart.
explanation.definitionFit: A swain is an archaic or poetic word for a young male lover or suitor who courts and accompanies a woman.

clue.text: African director Lee arranging loan

indicators.note: to arrange things is to set them in a new order, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: Ang Lee is the Taiwanese-born film director of Brokeback Mountain
taken as written

explanation.surface: A film director is busy setting up financing for an African project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lee' tempts one toward Spike, but the director's first name is what goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: An Angolan is a person from Angola, a country in southern Africa, so the adjective and noun both fit.

clue.text: Near bloody revolting snake

indicators.note: to revolt is to turn over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: near is an old British word for stingy, as is mean
blood is red

explanation.surface: Someone is warning that a horrible snake is close by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Near' looks like a location but is the dated British sense 'tight-fisted'; 'snake' looks like a noun but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To snake is to wind along a twisting course, exactly what a river does when it wanders in loops.

clue.text: 21, I've swum across small lake

indicators.note: something that has swum has moved about freely, so the letters are churned up
to lie across something is to span it, so one piece stretches around another

blocks.note: the answer to 21 across
taken as written
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Someone admits a blunder: they have swum across a small lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small lake' reads as one phrase, but 'small' is wordplay and 'lake' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A reservoir is a large artificial lake built to store water for supply, so the two are near synonyms.

clue.text: Regular departures from Kennedy terminal

indicators.note: leaving at regular intervals means taking every other letter in turn

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A timetable for scheduled flights out of JFK airport terminal.
explanation.walkthrough: The airport picture makes 'terminal' a building, but here it is the word for the final point.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminal is the end of a line or route, the last stop where something finishes.

clue.text: Working at The Ritz, all obey a Hollywood legend

indicators.note: working at something is labouring on it, so the following letters are worked into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: At a grand London hotel every member of staff bows to a visiting film star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working at' looks like part of the job description; 'at' belongs to the indicator, not the letters. The Ritz is a famously luxurious London hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Taylor was a leading star of classic Hollywood films such as Cleopatra, an iconic screen figure.

clue.text: A bit upset, OK, about packing an old crate

indicators.note: in a down entry, upsetting turns things upside down so they read bottom to top
turned about means facing the opposite way, so these letters run backwards
to pack something is to stuff it inside, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a tad is a small bit
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone, a little shaken, reassures us they are fine while loading a crate.
explanation.walkthrough: Crate is slang for a rickety old aeroplane, not a box. The Douglas Dakota was the RAF name for the wartime DC-3 transport.
explanation.definitionFit: The Douglas Dakota is a vintage twin-engined transport aircraft, and pilots' slang calls any ageing plane a crate.

clue.text: Horny individual's New Year in the French style

blocks.note: standard abbreviation of New Year
à la is French for 'in the style of'

explanation.surface: Someone randy celebrates New Year with Gallic flair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horny' suggests lust, but it means simply having horns.
explanation.definitionFit: The nyala is a southern African antelope whose males carry long spiralled horns, so it is literally horned.

clue.text: One's used to shift clothes cool model collected

indicators.note: to collect something is to gather it up and hold it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: gear is informal for clothing
sick is slang for excellent or cool
the Model T Ford, as in 22 across

explanation.surface: A fashion model gathers up clothes needed for a quick change between shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shift clothes' suggests changing outfits, but 'shift' goes with the definition: what a driver uses to change gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A gear stick is the lever a driver moves to change gear in a manual car, the British term for a gearshift.

clue.text: No longer tied up, ex-husband Jeremy went fishing

indicators.note: ex means former or out of, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: Jeremy Hunt is a British Conservative politician
H is the abbreviation for husband
to angle is to fish with a rod

explanation.surface: A divorced woman's former husband, free at last, went off fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ex-husband' reads as one word, but it means 'without H'. Jeremy Hunt is a senior British Conservative, once Chancellor of the Exchequer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untangled has had its knots and snarls worked free, so it is no longer knotted or bound up.

clue.text: 2's back to take over Sunday lunch

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in reverse
to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: 2 down is IVAN THE TERRIBLE, who was a tsar
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Ivan is back to host the family's Sunday lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference supplies a title rather than a name: 2 down was a tsar. In cricket, an over is a set of six balls.
explanation.definitionFit: A roast dinner of meat with potatoes and vegetables is the traditional British main meal served at midday on Sundays.

clue.text: Kraftwerk, REM, Lindisfarne touring Russian venue

indicators.note: a band on tour passes through places, so the word passes through the band names

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first name, all of the second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Three bands are on tour together, playing a Moscow venue.
explanation.walkthrough: Kraftwerk, REM and Lindisfarne are German, American and English bands; the touring picture makes the answer's seat of government sound like a concert hall.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kremlin is the fortified Moscow complex that houses the Russian government, jokingly called a venue.

clue.text: Los Angeles Times runs international hotel complex

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for the city
times as in multiplied by, as in three by four
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
a common abbreviation for international
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: The Los Angeles Times newspaper operates a global hotel resort.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Los Angeles Times' the newspaper, but it must be split; and 'hotel complex' must split too, as 'complex' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A labyrinth is an intricate maze, and complex as a noun means an intricate network of connected parts.

clue.text: He's often out on the tiles

definitions.text: He's often out on the tiles

blocks.clueFragment: He's often out on the tiles
blocks.note: surface reading: a man who regularly goes out partying at night
setter's reading: a tradesman who literally works outside, up on roof tiles

explanation.walkthrough: 'Out on the tiles' is a British idiom for a night of carousing; taken literally it describes a tradesman perched on a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: A roofer's job is laying and repairing roof tiles, so he spends much of his working day outdoors up on them.

clue.text: As Sánchez drops rising, inside political adviser

definitions.note: an example by description; the answer is a noun naming what Sánchez is

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading upward, so the letters go in reverse
being inside means enclosed by something else

blocks.note: rain falls in drops
a spad is British political slang for a special adviser to a minister

explanation.surface: Pedro Sánchez's poll numbers fall while they climb for someone else inside his team.
explanation.walkthrough: Pedro Sánchez is the Spanish prime minister; 'As' introduces the definition, meaning 'such as Sánchez is'. 'Drops' looks like a verb but is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedro Sánchez, Spain's prime minister, is a native of Spain, which is what the nationality noun names.

clue.text: Roughly beat silver leaves in this

indicators.note: doing something roughly means doing it carelessly, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Someone hammers silver leaf crudely, perhaps in a metal workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb or silver leaf, but it means tea leaves; the definition is a description of what the bag holds.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea bag is a small porous sachet holding tea leaves for brewing, so the leaves are in it.

clue.text: Okra on table; first impressions - it's rubbery

definitions.note: a playful definition: a rubber boot leaves footprints

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of each word that precedes it

blocks.note: gumbo is another name for okra
the initial letter of each word

explanation.surface: A food critic tastes okra on the table and finds it chewy at first bite.
explanation.walkthrough: Gumbo is okra, or the Louisiana stew thickened with it. A gumboot is the British word for a wellington, a rubber boot that leaves impressions.
explanation.definitionFit: A gumboot is a waterproof rubber boot, and its tread stamps impressions in mud, hence the cryptic description.

clue.text: Zeppelin songs? Cool!

blocks.note: airs are tunes or songs
hip means fashionable, cool

explanation.surface: Someone approves of Led Zeppelin's music.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites the rock band Led Zeppelin, but the definition is the German rigid airship.
explanation.definitionFit: A Zeppelin is a rigid dirigible built by the German Zeppelin company, the best-known kind of lighter-than-air craft.

clue.text: Contract card game (ace high)

blocks.note: A for ace, placed high, i.e. at the top of this down answer
bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: In contract bridge, the ace is the highest card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like part of 'contract bridge', the usual name for the game, but it is the verb meaning shorten.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a text is to shorten or condense it, so it is a synonym for contract in the sense of make smaller.

clue.text: Got very hot water in the Middle East when cycling

indicators.note: a cycle goes round, so letters from the front move round to the back

blocks.note: the Red Sea lies between Africa and Arabia

explanation.surface: Someone discovered the scalding water of a Middle Eastern sea while out on their bike.
explanation.walkthrough: Move the first three letters of RED SEA to the end. 'Cycling' suggests a bike ride, not rotation.
explanation.definitionFit: To be seared is to be scorched by intense heat, a past tense matching the verb phrase about becoming burning hot.

clue.text: Golfer Rory admits blunder

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the words contain the answer

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Rory McIlroy owns up to a mistake on the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admits' reads as confessing, but it means letting something in.
explanation.definitionFit: An error is a mistake, and a blunder is a careless or stupid mistake, so they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Famous American Model T vehicle

blocks.note: a mark is a model or version, as in a Mark II car
taken as written
a wain is an old word for a farm wagon

explanation.surface: Henry Ford's Model T, a famous American car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model T' reads as the Ford car, but splits into a model number and the letter. A wain is a hay wagon, as in Constable's painting The Hay Wain.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain, author of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn, is one of the most celebrated writers in United States history.

clue.text: Charge leaders of teachers organisation planning unauthorised protest

indicators.note: leaders are at the front, so the opening letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: the initial letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: Union heads are blamed for organising a wildcat strike by teachers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' looks like an accusation against the union leaders, but it means refill, as with a phone or battery.
explanation.definitionFit: To top up a phone or battery is to recharge it, filling it back to full capacity with credit or power.

clue.text: His band shot to fame where Isherwood lost his head

definitions.text: His band shot to fame where Isherwood lost his head

blocks.note: surface reading: a pop group's frontman whose band became famous; setter's reading: an outlaw whose men were renowned archers
behead the novelist's surname and the forest where the outlaw and his merry men lived appears

explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' and 'shot' suggest pop music, but the band is a gang of outlaws who shot arrows. Remove the I from Isherwood to reach Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary English outlaw led his merry men, famous archers, from their hideout in Sherwood Forest.

clue.text: Dance coach from Germany endlessly pirouetted, with Anton's lead

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
a pirouette is a full spin, turning the letters to face the other way
the lead is the one at the front, so the opening letter is used

blocks.note: Jürgen Klopp is the German football manager, formerly of Liverpool
the initial letter of the name

explanation.surface: A German trainer spins on a dance show, led by a professional partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes Strictly Come Dancing, where Anton Du Beke is a professional; but the coach is a football manager.
explanation.definitionFit: The polka is a lively Bohemian dance for couples in two-four time, popular across nineteenth-century Europe.

clue.text: Colour to fade, reportedly

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than seen, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: to die away is to fade

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a colour is said to be losing its brightness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colour' looks like the subject of fading, but it is the definition, as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To dye cloth or hair is to change its colour by soaking it in a pigment, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: "Deport them!" ordered Farage, finally entering likely to blow his top

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word
something entering goes inside, so a letter is put in among the others
when items are ordered they are put into a new sequence, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the closing letter of the surname

explanation.surface: Nigel Farage, the British anti-immigration politician, angrily demands deportations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' reads as Farage giving a command, but it tells the solver to rearrange the letters once the E is in.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot-tempered person is quick to anger, and blowing one's top is the idiom for losing one's temper explosively.
